Senses.Explanation: To take up the mallet and raise the whisk names the exact named speaker’s visible handling of teaching-seat implements while presiding, questioning, or answering before an assembly. Yunmen Wenyan describes teachers in other quarters making this display and asking whether people understand, then proposes a reply and a blow. Xuansha Shibei uses the same visible act in his test of how one receives blind, deaf, and mute interlocutors; the blind person cannot see it. Pin Jixiang treats the display as something contemporary teachers take pride in. Baichi Yuanshuo says his own use has no other purpose than announcing who he is, while Huazang Anmin proposes a scriptural account of the usual gesture and is laughed out of that resting place by Yuanwu Keqin. An unnamed monk challenges Xuefeng Yicun over whether the display suits higher teaching, and Xuefeng answers by raising the whisk. The phrase identifies an institutional teaching-seat action and its public visibility. The following words and responses vary, so the entry assigns no single hidden message to every lift of mallet or whisk.
